5. //
6. // This file contains specification functions and view types.

8. verus! {

10. use crate::hal::mem::spec_page_size;
11. use vstd::map::*;
12. 
13. pub uninterp spec fn byte_at_address(ptr: int) -> u8;
14. 
15. /// Abstract view of the frame allocator (`frame::Inner`).
16. ///
17. /// Captures which physical frames are currently allocated vs. free,
18. /// together with a per-frame reference count that models shared
19. /// ownership (e.g. copy-on-write after `share()`).
20. pub struct FrameAllocView
21. {
22.     pub allocated_frames: Set<int>,
23.     pub free_frames: Set<int>,
24.     /// Maps each allocated frame address to its reference count.
25.     /// A frame is present in the map iff it is currently allocated.
26.     pub refcounts: Map<int, int>,
27. }
28. 
29. impl FrameAllocView
30. {
31.     pub open spec fn wf(&self) -> bool
32.     {
33.         // Page-alignment
34.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.allocated_frames.contains(addr) ==> addr % spec_page_size() == 0
35.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.free_frames.contains(addr) ==> addr % spec_page_size() == 0
36.         // Disjoint
37.         &&& self.allocated_frames.disjoint(self.free_frames)
38.         // Allocated ↔ refcount consistency: a frame is allocated iff it has a positive refcount
39.         &&& forall|addr: int| #[trigger] self.allocated_frames.contains(addr) <==>
40.             self.refcounts.contains_key(addr) && self.refcounts[addr] > 0
41.         // Free frames have no refcount entry
42.         &&& forall|addr: int| #[trigger] self.free_frames.contains(addr) ==>
43.             !self.refcounts.contains_key(addr)
44.         // Refcount bounded by u8 range
45.         &&& forall|addr: int| self.refcounts.contains_key(addr) ==>
46.             0 < self.refcounts[addr] <= 255
47.     }
48. }
49. 
50. } // end verus!
51.

54. //==================================================================================================

56. // vstd does not provide a specification for `alloc::collections::LinkedList`. Verified functions in
57. // this module (`init`) take `LinkedList` parameters, so Verus needs to know the type. We declare it
58. // as an opaque external type. We deliberately do NOT provide a `View`/iterator specification: doing
59. // so requires implementing vstd's `View`/`ForLoopGhostIterator` traits for the foreign std types

84. 
85. /// Abstract state of the global physical-memory subsystem managed by `mm::phys`.
86. ///
87. /// Models the boot lifecycle of the frame-allocator singleton plus its
88. /// frame-reservation state. The `frames` component mirrors `frame::instance()@`;
89. /// the `initialized` flag mirrors the `INSTANCE_INIT` lifecycle gate.
90. pub struct PhysMemView {
91.     /// Whether the frame-allocator singleton has been established
92.     /// (i.e. `init` ran once and returned `Ok`). Models one-shot/monotonic
93.     /// boot: `false` before `init`, `true` after a successful `init`.
94.     pub initialized: bool,
95.     /// Abstract reservation state of the global frame allocator: which physical
96.     /// frames are reserved (allocated) vs. free, with per-frame refcounts.
97.     /// Meaningful (well-formed) only once `initialized` is `true`.
98.     pub frames: FrameAllocView,
99. }
100. 
101. impl PhysMemView {
102.     /// Well-formedness: once the allocator is established, the frame-allocator
103.     /// invariant holds. Before initialization there is no allocator, so no
104.     /// constraint applies.
105.     pub open spec fn inv(self) -> bool {
106.         self.initialized ==> self.frames.wf()
107.     }
108. 
109.     /// Frames the allocator actually tracks (covered by the bitmap): the union
110.     /// of reserved and free frames. The abstract form of `is_covered`.
111.     pub open spec fn covered(self) -> Set<int> {
112.         self.frames.allocated_frames.union(self.frames.free_frames)
113.     }
114. 
115.     /// The set of frame addresses occupied by a region `[start, start+size)`.
116.     pub open spec fn region_frames(start: int, size: int) -> Set<int> {
117.         let first = start / spec_page_size();
118.         let last = (start + size) / spec_page_size();
119.         set_int_range(first, last).map(|i: int| i * spec_page_size())
120.     }
121. 
122.     /// `init` established the allocator from the caller-supplied bitmap state;
123.     /// lifecycle flips on.
124.     pub open spec fn spec_initialize(self, initial: FrameAllocView) -> PhysMemView {
125.         PhysMemView { initialized: true, frames: initial }
126.     }
127. 
128.     /// Book one covered frame: move `addr` from free to allocated, refcount = 1.
129.     /// Mirrors `Inner::book`'s `Ok` post-state.
130.     pub open spec fn spec_book_frame(self, addr: int) -> PhysMemView {
131.         PhysMemView {
132.             frames: FrameAllocView {
133.                 allocated_frames: self.frames.allocated_frames.insert(addr),
134.                 free_frames: self.frames.free_frames.remove(addr),
135.                 refcounts: self.frames.refcounts.insert(addr, 1int),
136.             },
137.             ..self
138.         }
139.     }
140. 
141.     /// Book a set of frames at once: move them all from free to allocated, each
142.     /// with refcount = 1. Mirrors `Inner::alloc_range`'s `Ok` post-state and
143.     /// generalizes it from a contiguous region to an arbitrary frame set.
144.     pub open spec fn spec_book_frames(self, frames: Set<int>) -> PhysMemView {
145.         PhysMemView {
146.             frames: FrameAllocView {
147.                 allocated_frames: self.frames.allocated_frames.union(frames),
148.                 free_frames: self.frames.free_frames.difference(frames),
149.                 refcounts: self.frames.refcounts.union_prefer_right(
150.                     Map::new(|a: int| frames.contains(a), |a: int| 1int),
151.                 ),
152.             },
153.             ..self
154.         }
155.     }
156. }
157. 
158. /// Abstract view of the global physical-memory subsystem at the current program
159. /// point.
160. ///
161. /// The subsystem state lives in module-level `static`s (`frame::INSTANCE` /
162. /// `frame::INSTANCE_INIT`) that a Verus `spec fn` cannot read directly, so this
163. /// is an *uninterpreted* function: the exec wrappers in `frame.rs` and the
164. /// `book_*`/`init` functions pin down its value through their `ensures` clauses.
165. /// `initialized` mirrors `INSTANCE_INIT`; `frames` mirrors `frame::instance()@`.
166. ///
167. /// This is the handle the caller-facing contract of `init` is stated over: after
168. /// a successful `init`, `phys_view().initialized` and `phys_view().inv()` hold, so
169. /// every later `frame::*` / `PhysMemoryManager::*` operation may rely on the
170. /// frame-allocator invariant.
171. pub uninterp spec fn phys_view() -> PhysMemView;
172. 
173. } // end verus!

59. // This function iterates the supplied `LinkedList` of regions. The std `LinkedList`
60. // iterator cannot be given a Verus `for`-loop specification from this crate (the orphan
61. // rule forbids implementing vstd's iterator traits for the foreign `Iter` type, and the
62. // pinned `vstd` dependency cannot be extended — see `mod.spec.rs` / `verus-unsupported.md`).
63. // The function is therefore `external_body`; its `#[verus_spec]` contract is honored by the
64. // caller (`init`). The abstract effect — every frame of every region becomes booked — is
65. // modelled by `PhysMemView::spec_book_frames` / `region_frames` and discharged by
66. // `lemma_book_region_reserves_region_frames` in `mod.proof.rs`. Because the region frames are
67. // the contents of the (un-viewable) `LinkedList`, they cannot be enumerated in this boundary
68. // contract; what is expressed is the caller-relevant guarantee that the allocator stays
69. // initialized and well-formed across booking.
70. #[verus_spec(result =>
71.     requires
72.         phys_view().initialized,
73.         phys_view().inv(),
74.     ensures
75.         phys_view().inv(),
76.         match result {
77.             Ok(()) => phys_view().initialized,
78.             Err(_) => true,
79.         },
80. )]
81. fn book_physical_memory_regions(
82.     physical_memory_regions: LinkedList<TruncatedMemoryRegion<PhysicalAddress>>,
83. ) -> Result<(), Error> {
84.     info!("booking physical memory regions ...");
85. 
86.     // Book physical memory that is not usable.
87.     for region in physical_memory_regions.iter() {
88.         info!("booking: {:?}", region);
89.         frame::alloc_range(region)?;
90.     }
91. 
92.     Ok(())
93. }
94. 
95. // `external_body` for the same std-`LinkedList` reason as
96. // `book_physical_memory_regions`; its `#[verus_spec]` contract is honored by the caller
97. // (`init`). The abstract effect — every *tracked* MMIO frame (`is_covered`) becomes booked
98. // while untracked frames are skipped — is modelled by `PhysMemView::spec_book_frames` over
99. // `M.intersect(covered())` and discharged by `lemma_book_mmio_skip_untracked` /
100. // `lemma_book_mmio_books_tracked` in `mod.proof.rs`. As with the physical-region helper, the
101. // concrete MMIO frame set is the contents of the (un-viewable) `LinkedList`, so the boundary
102. // contract expresses the caller-relevant guarantee: the allocator stays initialized and
103. // well-formed (the skip-if-not-covered tolerance never aborts boot).
104. #[verus_spec(result =>
105.     requires
106.         phys_view().initialized,
107.         phys_view().inv(),
108.     ensures
109.         phys_view().inv(),
110.         match result {
111.             Ok(()) => phys_view().initialized,
112.             Err(_) => true,
113.         },
114. )]
115. fn book_mmio_regions(
116.     mmio_regions: &LinkedList<TruncatedMemoryRegion<VirtualAddress>>,
117. ) -> Result<(), Error> {
118.     info!("booking memory-mapped i/o regions ...");
119. 
120.     // Book memory-mapped I/O regions.
121.     for region in mmio_regions.iter() {
122.         info!("booking: {:?}", region);
123.         let mut start: usize = region.start().into_raw_value();
124.         let end: usize = start + (region.size() - 1);
125.         while start < end {
126.             let mmio_addr: usize = crate::hal::platform::gva_to_gpa(start);
127.             let phys_addr: PageAligned<PhysicalAddress> = PageAligned::from_address(unsafe {
128.                 // MMIO GPAs may legitimately lie outside tracked RAM, so they must not go through
129.                 // the regular physical-address validator here.
130.                 PhysicalAddress::from_mmio_address(VirtualAddress::from_raw_value(mmio_addr))?
131.             })?;
132. 
133.             // Only book frames that the frame allocator actually tracks.
134.             // MMIO regions above RAM (e.g. the LAPIC at 0xFEE0_0000) are not
135.             // covered by the bitmap and must be skipped.
136.             if frame::is_covered(phys_addr) {
137.                 frame::book(phys_addr)?;
138.             }
139.             start += mem::FRAME_SIZE;
140.         }
141.     }
142. 
143.     Ok(())
144. }
145. 
146. ///
147. /// # Description
148. ///
149. /// Initializes the physical memory manager.
150. ///
151. /// # Parameters
152. ///
153. /// - `physical_memory_regions`: Physical memory regions to book.
154. /// - `mmio_regions`: Memory-mapped I/O regions to book.
155. /// - `physical_memory_layout`: Physical memory layout bitmap.
156. ///
157. /// # Returns
158. ///
159. /// Upon success, `Ok(())` is returned. Upon failure, an error is returned instead.
160. ///
161. #[verus_spec(ret =>
162.     ensures
163.         // The frame-allocator invariant is established/preserved on every path: this
164.         // is the precondition every later `frame::*` / `PhysMemoryManager::*` call
165.         // relies on. (Vacuous before the allocator becomes initialized.)
166.         phys_view().inv(),
167.         match ret {
168.             // One-shot boot success: the global subsystem is now initialized and its
169.             // reservation state is well-formed, so reserved frames (allocated) are
170.             // disjoint from the free pool and can never be handed out by `alloc`.
171.             Ok(()) => {
172.                 &&& phys_view().initialized
173.                 &&& phys_view().frames.allocated_frames.disjoint(phys_view().frames.free_frames)
174.             },
175.             // Failure is terminal for the boot path; no completeness of reservation is
176.             // promised, only that the invariant still holds (checked above).
177.             Err(_) => true,
178.         },
179. )]
180. pub fn init(
181.     physical_memory_regions: LinkedList<TruncatedMemoryRegion<PhysicalAddress>>,
182.     mmio_regions: &LinkedList<TruncatedMemoryRegion<VirtualAddress>>,
183.     physical_memory_layout: Bitmap,
184. ) -> Result<(), Error> {
185.     // Initialize frame allocator singleton.
186.     info!("initializing the frame allocator ...");
187.     // Safety: called exactly once during single-threaded boot.
188.     unsafe { frame::init(physical_memory_layout)? };
189.     book_physical_memory_regions(physical_memory_regions)?;
190. 
191.     book_mmio_regions(mmio_regions)?;
192. 
193.     // Initialize user page pool.
194.     info!("initializing the user page pool ...");
195.     let upool: Upool = Upool::new();
196. 
197.     // Initialize physical memory manager singleton.
198.     info!("initializing the physical memory manager ...");
199.     PhysMemoryManager::init(upool)?;
200. 
201.     Ok(())
202. }

description: "Mandatory rules for writing Verus code. Covers attribute-based syntax, source integrity for exec code, forbidden patterns, and assume_specification policy. Must be followed whenever producing or modifying Verus-annotated code."

# Verus Constraints

## Attribute Style for Exec Functions

All specs on **exec functions** must use the attribute-based syntax
(`#[verus_spec]`, `#[verus_verify]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`).
See the **verus-syntax** skill for the full reference and examples.

```rust
// ✅ CORRECT — attribute style for exec functions
#[verus_spec(ret =>
    requires x < 100,
    ensures ret == x + 1,
)]
fn foo(x: u32) -> u32 {
    x + 1
}

// ❌ WRONG — do not wrap exec functions in verus! { }
verus! {
    fn foo(x: u32) -> (ret: u32)
        requires x < 100,
        ensures ret == x + 1,
    { x + 1 }
} // verus!
```

**`verus! { }` blocks** are still used for:
- `spec fn` and `proof fn` definitions (in `.spec.rs` and `.proof.rs`)
- Type-level specs (`broadcast`, `impl View`, etc.)

Key benefit: exec function signatures stay unmodified — the original `fn`
signature is untouched, specs live in the attribute.

## Source Integrity (exec code)

The following rules apply to the original source files (e.g. `lib.rs`), not to
`*.spec.rs` / `*.proof.rs` which are freely editable.

Verus verification is **in-place**: specs and proofs are added directly alongside
exec code. The annotated code remains fully compilable and runnable — Verus
constructs are erased during normal `cargo build` via cfg-gating. Keep changes
minimal so developers can review diffs easily.

**Preserve by default:** exec logic, function signatures, struct definitions,
comments, debug assertions, and all other existing code.

The escalation ladder (each step requires exhausting the previous):

1. **Verify as-is** — most code works with Verus directly.
2. **Search vstd** — your training data is likely outdated. `grep -r` the entire
   vstd directory broadly (see "vstd & Common Misconceptions" section below).
3. If verification still fails after steps 1–2, try different proof
   strategies (add lemmas, intermediate assertions, split into smaller
   functions). If Verus reports that a **syntax construct is unsupported**
   (not a proof failure and not a missing spec for a stdlib function),
   record it in `verus-unsupported.md` with the exact error message and
   the minimal code that triggers it. Do NOT rewrite exec code, add
   `external_body`, or add `assume_specification` to work around it.

**The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully compatible with Verus.**
There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Any
verification failure is a proof issue, not a Verus limitation. Do NOT
rewrite exec code, add `external_body` — these are never needed.

**Never cfg-gate away and duplicate exec definitions.** Adding
`#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` to a function, impl block, struct, enum, or
constant and providing a verus-annotated copy is forbidden — it verifies the
copy, not the real code, and the two will silently diverge.

- **Functions / impl blocks**: add contracts to the original in-place.
- **Structs / enums**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If a
  derive macro is incompatible, cfg-gate only the derive attribute, not
  the struct. If the struct truly cannot be parsed by Verus, use
  `external_type_specification` in spec.rs to declare it — do not
  duplicate the definition. Write `external_type_specification` **once**
  in the crate/module that defines the type; other modules `use` it.
- **Constants**: Verus sees the original definition directly. If Verus
  cannot resolve a constant from another workspace module, add
  `#[verus_verify]` to the defining module. Never
  `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` the original constant.

**Allowed additions:** `#[verus_spec(...)]` and `#[verus_verify]` attributes,
`proof! { }` / `proof_decl! { }` / `proof_with! { }` macros, `#[verus_spec(...)]`
on loops, `verus! { }` blocks (for spec/proof fn in .spec.rs/.proof.rs),
vstd imports (cfg-gated), ghost/tracked local variables (each must be
used by at least one proof construct — assertion, invariant, or proof block),
`Ghost<T>` / `Tracked<T>` struct fields (only when proof requires ghost
state to flow through exec code — prefer keeping ghost state in View),
`#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(...))]` gating.

**After completing all changes**, use the `ast-consistency` skill to verify
source integrity. Fix all inconsistencies.

## Forbidden Patterns

| Pattern | Policy |
|---|---|
| `admit()` | Allowed during specification phase as a placeholder. Must be eliminated during proving phase |
| `assume(...)` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external_body]` | **On current module's own functions**: unconditionally forbidden in all phases — `admit()` in a proof body is the correct placeholder during specification (it skips only the proof obligation while Verus still checks exec code; `external_body` skips everything). **On dependency functions in other modules**: allowed as a temporary contract placeholder while the dependency is not yet verified. Must be removed when the dependency module is verified |
| `#[verifier::trusted]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::external]` | Banned — not needed under attribute style (only `#[verus_verify]`-annotated items are checked) |
| `#[verifier::exec_allows_no_decreases_clause]` | Banned |
| `#[verifier::spinoff_prover]` | Banned — even if verification passes with spinoff, the proof is fragile and will break with minor changes. Improve the proof itself |
| `#[verifier::rlimit(N)]` | Timeout means the proof is too weak — simplify the proof, split lemmas, add intermediate assertions. Never use rlimit to work around timeouts. If all proof strategies are exhausted and the proof is genuinely optimal, rlimit up to 50 is the absolute maximum |
| `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` on exec code | **Cheating** — cfg-gating branches, expressions, match arms, or code blocks means Verus verifies different code than what runs. Only allowed on non-semantic items: `derive(...)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`), and imports |
| `uninterp spec fn` | **Banned** — all spec functions must have concrete definitions. Using `uninterp` to avoid writing a concrete spec is cheating — it has the same effect as `assume` when paired with `external_body` proof axioms |

## cfg_attr and verus_keep_ghost

- **Do NOT wrap any Verus attribute or proof macro in `cfg_attr(verus_keep_ghost, ...)`, and do NOT guard one with `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`.** This applies to `#[verus_spec(...)]`, `#[verus_verify(...)]`, `proof! { }`, `proof_decl! { }`, and `proof_with! { }`. These constructs are *already ghost*: the macros erase themselves during a normal (non-Verus) `cargo build` and only take effect under `verus_keep_ghost`, so an extra `verus_keep_ghost` gate is redundant and wrong. Write them directly.
- **`use vstd::prelude::*;` must NOT be cfg-gated** — do not add `#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]`. This import must be unconditionally present so that Verus-specific constructs (e.g. `#[verus_spec]`, `proof!{}`) are properly parsed and erased during normal `cargo build`.

See **verus-syntax** skill for correct examples.

## Warnings

Verus verification must produce **zero warnings**. Two most common:

- **Missing trigger** — add `#[trigger]` on the relevant expression inside
  the quantifier, or annotate the quantifier with `#[auto]` to let Verus
  choose triggers automatically.
- **Incompatible derive** — `#[cfg_attr(not(verus_keep_ghost), derive(Clone, Debug, ...))]`
  to gate out derives that Verus cannot process.

## Trust Boundaries (pre-approved TCB)

Trust boundaries — calls to code outside the verification scope whose
implementation cannot be verified (hardware registers, inline assembly, MMIO,
FFI, std library internals, external systems) — are the external-bottom
boundary. Which functions are trusted is **fixed in advance** by the TCB allowed
list (`tcb-allowed.md`). Do NOT introduce, justify, or record new trust
boundaries during specification or proving: if a function is not already in the
TCB allowed list, it must be fully verified or eliminated.

Mechanisms that rely on the TCB (`assume_specification`, `external_body`,
`axiom`) are only permitted on functions already in the allowed list.

**Do NOT use trust to hide proof failures.** If a function cannot be verified
after exhausting all proof strategies but is not in the TCB allowed list,
record it in `verification-todo.md` (in the logs directory) instead:

```markdown
## verification-todo.md entry format
- Function: `Foo::bar` (file.rs:42)
- Status: UNPROVEN
- Attempts: (list strategies tried)
- Blocker: (describe why verification fails)
```

These are tracked separately so they are never mistaken for accepted trust
assumptions. The goal is to return and resolve them — not to accept them.

Recording a function here does **not** make verification pass: the cheating
gate ignores `verification-todo.md`, and any remaining `admit()` / `assume()`
still fails the gate. This file is an honest hand-off of genuinely-stuck
proofs — never an escape hatch for giving up.

## assume_specification

`assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.

**Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).

**Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

## Trust Boundaries (pre-approved TCB)

Trust boundaries — calls to code outside the verification scope whose
implementation cannot be verified (hardware registers, inline assembly, MMIO,
FFI, std library internals, external systems) — are the external-bottom
boundary. Which functions are trusted is **fixed in advance** by the TCB allowed
list (`tcb-allowed.md`). Do NOT introduce, justify, or record new trust
boundaries during specification or proving: if a function is not already in the
TCB allowed list, it must be fully verified or eliminated.

Mechanisms that rely on the TCB (`assume_specification`, `external_body`,
`axiom`) are only permitted on functions already in the allowed list.

**Do NOT use trust to hide proof failures.** If a function cannot be verified
after exhausting all proof strategies but is not in the TCB allowed list,
record it in `verification-todo.md` (in the logs directory) instead:

```markdown
## verification-todo.md entry format
- Function: `Foo::bar` (file.rs:42)
- Status: UNPROVEN
- Attempts: (list strategies tried)
- Blocker: (describe why verification fails)
```

These are tracked separately so they are never mistaken for accepted trust
assumptions. The goal is to return and resolve them — not to accept them.

Recording a function here does **not** make verification pass: the cheating
gate ignores `verification-todo.md`, and any remaining `admit()` / `assume()`
still fails the gate. This file is an honest hand-off of genuinely-stuck
proofs — never an escape hatch for giving up.

## assume_specification

`assume_specification` provides specs for std library or external functions
whose body Verus cannot verify (because vstd does not include them).
These are **external-bottom** trust assumptions (see **spec-design** skill) —
unverified axioms that, if wrong, make downstream proofs unsound.

**Allowed** for std library / external functions not covered by vstd.
Follow the audit checklist in `spec-design` (documentation fidelity, soft
contract coverage, no stronger than the API, version sensitivity).

**Before writing:** search vstd for existing specs of that function,
search verified dependency specs for reusable `assume_specification`,
look for safe Verus API alternatives, try restructuring to avoid the call.

vstd is rapidly evolving — specs you believe are missing may already exist.
**Your training data is likely outdated.** Before concluding that a std
function has no spec or that a construct is unsupported, you **must** search
the actual vstd source thoroughly:

```bash
grep -r "function_name" /path/to/vstd/        # broad search
grep -r "spec.*fn.*method" /path/to/vstd/     # spec function patterns
```

two files. Look in `vstd/std_specs/`, `vstd/seq*.rs`, `vstd/map*.rs`,
`vstd/set*.rs`, `vstd/arithmetic/`, `vstd/raw_ptr.rs`, etc.

- **Verus supports `for` loops** — do not replace with `while` unless semantically appropriate.
- **Don't hallucinate syntax** — when unsure, check the Verus reference or vstd examples.

**The exec code has been pre-refactored to be fully Verus-compatible.**
There are no known Verus front-end limitations in the codebase. Do NOT
claim any construct is unsupported, rewrite exec code, add `external_body`,
or use `// VERUS REWRITE`. Any verification failure is a proof issue —
strengthen the proof, do not change the code.

### Guardrails

**Cfg-gating exec code is cheating.** `#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]` is only
appropriate for non-semantic items that Verus truly cannot parse:
`derive(Debug)`, `debug_assert!`, logging macros (`info!`, `error!`).
Do NOT cfg-gate match arms, closures, large code blocks, or expressions.
This makes Verus verify different code than what actually runs.

**Anti-pattern — body duplication (absolutely forbidden):**

```rust
// ❌ WRONG: real body hidden from Verus, replaced with different code
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> {
    #[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
    { /* real implementation */ }
    #[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
    { /* different code that Verus can parse */ }
}
```

**Anti-pattern — function duplication (absolutely forbidden):**

```rust
// ❌ WRONG: entire function gated out, replaced with a different definition
#[cfg(not(verus_keep_ghost))]
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* real */ }
#[cfg(verus_keep_ghost)]
fn foo(&mut self, x: usize) -> Result<(), Error> { /* different */ }
```

Both patterns verify a **different program** than what ships. The proof is
meaningless. Find a single body that both Rust and Verus accept.

name: proving-guide
description: "Proving methodology and mindset for Verus verification: function-by-function approach, persistence through failures, clean verification, and bug reporting. Use when writing proofs or resolving verification failures."
---

# Proving Guide

Read `verus-constraints` first. See `verus-syntax` for attribute-based syntax
reference. Study `docs/examples/binary-search/proof/` for a working example.

## Core Approach

1. **One function at a time.** Resolve `admit()` function by function,
   following the order from the `verification-order` skill if a
   verification plan exists. Do not move to the next function until the
   current one verifies cleanly.
   
   The current module's functions must NOT have `external_body`.
   Do NOT add `external_body` to any function during proving.

2. **Keep trying.** When verification fails, read the error log carefully,
   try a different proof strategy, and iterate. You are capable of solving
   this — if one approach fails, try the next. Do not give up or ask for
   suggestions; work through possible approaches systematically.

3. **Never weaken specs.** If a spec is hard to prove, the proof strategy
   is wrong — not the spec. Do not relax `requires`, weaken `ensures`,
   or remove clauses to make proofs easier. The spec is the contract.

4. **Report genuine bugs.** If after thorough attempts you determine the
   failure is caused by a code bug (not a proof gap), report it immediately
   using the `bug-reporting` skill. Do not silently work around code bugs.

5. **Clean verification.** After all proofs pass, check for warnings and
   resolve them. A clean verification has zero errors AND zero warnings.
   Trigger warnings are especially common and must not be left: add
   explicit `#[trigger]` annotations or restructure quantifiers until
   all trigger warnings are gone.

## Verification Tool

Use `make verify-<crate> MODULE=<module>` to verify the current module during
proving. After all modules are done, run `make verify-<crate>` (no MODULE) to
confirm the full crate still passes. The output includes:
- **Verification result** — pass/fail with error details
- **Cheating detection** — flags `admit`, `assume`, `external_body`, `trusted`,
  cfg-gated exec code; all must be resolved in current module.
  `external_body` on direct callees in dependency modules is expected
  until those modules are verified; **Never** mark callers
  (upstream modules) as `external_body`
- **Coverage** — which functions have contracts

After verification passes, use the `ast-consistency` skill to check that
exec code was not accidentally modified during proving. Fix all
inconsistencies before finalizing.

---

## Proof Organization

- **Write proof helpers in `.proof.rs` from the start.** If a proof block
  would exceed ~5 lines, don't write it inline — define a `proof fn` in the
  `.proof.rs` file and call it from the inline `proof { }` block. Same for
  loop invariants with more than ~5 clauses: define a `spec fn` predicate in
  `.proof.rs` and reference it in the `invariant` clause. This avoids
  cluttering exec code and eliminates extraction work later.
- Keep proof fn granular: one lemma per function, chain via `assert ... by { lemma_call(); }`
- Default: make specs `opaque`, only `reveal()` where needed

## Inductive Invariants

Functions with loops or recursion need inductive invariants — without them
Verus cannot verify the function. If loop invariants already exist, review
them before attempting the proof. When `admit()` is removed, existing
invariants may turn out to be too weak. Strengthen them — do not work
around the failure with cheating. If no invariant exists yet, define one
before attempting the proof.

1. **Review the existing invariant.** Read the `invariant` clause (or the
   `spec fn` it references). Understand what it claims and what it misses.
2. **Strengthen as needed.** Add missing clauses or tighten existing ones
   based on Verus error messages. Getting the invariant right on the first
   try is rare — iterate until it passes. Never bypass a failing obligation
   with `admit`, `assume`, or `external_body`.
3. **Verify the three obligations:**
   - **Base case** — the invariant holds on entry (before the first
     iteration, or for the base constructor).
   - **Inductive step** — if the invariant holds before an iteration /
     recursive call, it holds after.
   - **Sufficiency** — the invariant, combined with the loop exit
     condition, implies the postcondition.
